newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Change in Hong Kong administration comes early.
newsitem.headline: Change in Hong Kong administration comes early.

text.p: Hong Kong's handover from Britain to China is starting to take effect six months ahead of schedule after the outgoing colonial governor's deputy promised to continue serving under the incoming chief executive.

A cartoon in Sunday's Hong Kong Standard summed it up -- Governor Chris Patten stands aghast by a jalopy with flat tyres and hissing radiator as Chief Secretary Anson Chan nips into an open-top sports car driven by future leader Tung Chee-hwa.

Chan, Patten's popular second-in-command and the senior civil servant in a territory where the bureaucracy has extraordinary powers, said on Saturday after a meeting with Tung that she had received and accepted a request to stay on.
"In effect this is the change of regime that we're seeing here," political analyst Michael DeGolyer of Hong Kong's Baptist University told Reuters on Sunday.

Chan's continuation in office comes as no surprise -- both she and Tung, the shipping tycoon chosen to become Hong Kong's future leader earlier this month by a 400-member Beijing-backed committee, had previously made clear they each wished it.

But the confirmation has been welcomed widely as good for confidence in Hong Kong's transition just before the dawn of 1997 -- the year that sees the end of more than 150 years of British colonial rule when China takes over on July 1.
"So Hong Kong is to get its 'dream team'," the South China Morning Post said in its Sunday editorial.

"Just as Mr Tung has come to epitomise a set of prudent, businesslike values and a non-confrontational style for the future, Mrs Chan stands for the continuity of good and effective administration ... it is difficult to envisage a better combination for the transition, not just internally but in terms of Hong Kong's international position," it said.
However, Chan's appointment could herald an early transfer of the civil service's loyalty, some analysts warned.

"From now on the entire administration from Anson Chan downward will just do everything that the chief executive designate says, because if they don't they're not going to have a future," said legislator and pro-democracy activist Emily Lau.

"I certainly hope something can be worked out because what we Hong Kong people want is a smooth transition, but we don't want a completely lame-duck and ineffectual administration or an administration that's completely beholden to Peking," she said.
In Hong Kong's executive-led administration, civil servants formulate and carry out policy. Legislators vote on laws and budgets drawn up by bureaucrats, but rarely initiate policy.

Local's civil servants have built up a reputation as effective and incorruptible, and their continued effectiveness, incorruptibility and freedom to get on with running things under Chinese sovereignty are seen as crucial for Hong Kong's future.

But Chan's continuation is also the start of what will be an extraordinary balancing act for her and the rest of the civil service given some of the deep differences between the British and Beijing, and could lead to a freeze in policy making.

The cleavage is starkest over Beijing's plan to replace the elected legislature with a provisional council that was chosen earlier this month by the same committee that chose Tung. The provisional body will hold its first informal meeting next week.
"In the coming period, civil servants will face parallel legislative structures," Ming Pao Daily warned in an editorial.
"If there are rapid policy changes before the handover, the government's policy-making units will be divided. The best way is to maintain policies without change during this period."
Chan has always echoed Patten's vehement opposition to the provisional council but few expect her to continue to do so publicly.
Baptist University's DeGolyer also warned uncertainty was not laid to rest by Chan's continuation in her position.
Once the Hong Kong administration holds promised fresh elections and installs an elected legislature in 1998, Tung may feel in a better position to make changes in the civil service.
"You have to remember that Anson Chan is not trusted by many of the pro-China groups (in Hong Kong)," he said. "She's certainly not trusted by the people of Beijing."
